near_miss.lead: Arm. gorcecʻakʻ ... zaynpisi mec ew ahawor gorc 'we did such a great and terrible deed' (+ an-gēt-s 'ignorant', an-xorhowrd 'without counsel') ~ Gk μέγα ῥέξαι ἔργον (Th. 209-10, with ἀτασθαλίῃ), μέγα ἔργον ... ἐμήσατ' (Od. 24.426); cf. Od. 11.272 μέγα ἔργον ἔρεξεν ἀιδρείῃσι νόοιο, where ἀ-ιδρείη matches Arm. an-gēt (*n̥-weyd-)
near_miss.why_not: The cognates hold (mec : μέγας, gorc : ἔργον, gorcem : ῥέζω), and the 'outrageous deed done in ignorance' sense is close to the Homeric one. But *meǵh2- + *wérǵom is everyday language: about 769 near-2 hits in Greek, 18 in Armenian (mostly positive: mec gorc 'great work'), and also ON mikit verk, OHG mihhil werk. There are none in Indo-Iranian. Lazar is 5th-c. Hellenizing Christian prose, so a calque or chance is more likely than inheritance.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_13_Lazar_Parp ed. page 2265 - PDF page 65 (word id 21892) (w2/3)
near_miss.lead: Arm. i towē ew i gišeri 'by day and by night' (tiw < *diw-, gišer < *wekʷsperos) ~ ORu dьnь ... večerъ (*dey-/*dyew-, *wekʷsperos)
near_miss.why_not: The Russian is not a merism: 'five days ... then it being evening'. The Arm. merism is the biblical ἡμέρας καὶ νυκτός and is generic.

near_miss.why_not: The senses differ: the Skt grants life to a suppliant, while the Arm. offers one's own self to death (Christian martyr idiom). The anjn < *h2enh1- etymology is uncertain, and 'give one's life' is generic.

near_miss.lead: Arm. ənd jer̄amb iwreancʻ ownin 'hold under their hand' ~ Gk ὑποχειρίους γενέσθαι 'come under the hand'
near_miss.why_not: This is a pan-European idiom of subjection (Lat. sub manu), very likely a Greek calque in Armenian, and the Thucydidean adjective is lexicalized.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_13_Lazar_Parp ed. page 2350 - PDF page 150 (word id 53777) (w3/4)
near_miss.lead: Simile of a warrior attacking like an eagle (arcowi < *h2r̥ǵipyós) on a flock of partridges, killing some and scattering the rest into rock clefts (also in Movses Khorenacʻi, ed. page 1920). Compare Homeric hawk/eagle-on-flock similes (Il. 15.690, 16.582, 17.460) and RV 4.38 ṛjipyá- of the war horse Dadhikrā
near_miss.why_not: The slab partners (Herodotus on mines) are irrelevant. The Greek similes use non-cognate αἰετός/ἴρηξ, and the Vedic ṛjipyá- (RV 4.38.2c, 7c) is an epithet with no flock-attack scene. So no cognate pair sits in a matching simile; there is a typological parallel only.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_2_13_Lazar_Parp ed. page 2352 - PDF page 152 (word id 54725) (w2/2)
near_miss.lead: In the context line after the passage, the slaughtered enemy is compared with reapers' swaths heaped close together (mangał, gerandi, orays mawt i mawt kowteal). Compare Il. 11.67-71 ἀμητῆρες ... δράγματα ταρφέα πίπτει
near_miss.why_not: No cognate material (the Arm. words are loans or isolated), the battle-harvest image is universal and biblical, and there is no partner in the bundle.
